subject: business-studies
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which statement about operating at 100% capacity utilisation is most accurate?
options: It is always ideal with no drawbacks
It minimises fixed cost per unit but leaves no slack for new orders or maintenance
questions.explain: Full utilisation spreads fixed costs thinly but leaves no spare capacity for extra orders, maintenance or breakdowns.

questions.q: Benchmarking involves:
options: Comparing a firm's processes or performance against best-practice rivals
questions.explain: Benchmarking compares a firm's performance or processes against the best in the industry to identify improvements.

questions.q: A bespoke wedding-cake maker producing one-off items to customer specification is best described as using which production process?
questions.explain: Job production makes single, unique items to individual customer specification.

questions.q: Kaizen refers to:
options: A radical, one-off redesign of operations
questions.explain: Kaizen is the philosophy of continuous, small-step improvement driven by employee involvement.

questions.q: A plant has a maximum output of 20,000 units but produces 15,000. What is its capacity utilisation?
questions.explain: Capacity utilisation = actual output ÷ maximum output × 100 = 15,000 ÷ 20,000 × 100 = 75%.

questions.q: Effective supply-chain management primarily aims to:
options: Get the right inputs in the right quantity, quality and time at lowest cost
Maximise the number of suppliers used
Eliminate the need for any inventory
questions.explain: Supply-chain management coordinates flows so the right inputs arrive in the right quality, quantity and time at minimum cost.

questions.q: A firm's operational flexibility refers to its ability to:
options: Adapt output type or volume to changing demand
questions.explain: Flexibility is the capacity to vary the type or volume of output in response to changing customer demand.

questions.q: Which best describes 'value' in supplier selection for operations?
options: Balancing price, quality, reliability and flexibility
Selecting the supplier with the largest order minimum
questions.explain: Choosing suppliers on value means weighing price against quality, reliability, flexibility and delivery, not price alone.

questions.q: A bakery makes 500 white loaves, then switches the line to 500 brown loaves, then to 500 rye. This is:
questions.explain: Producing groups of identical items in stages before switching to the next group is batch production.

questions.q: The main argument in favour of outsourcing a non-core activity is that it:
options: Lets the firm focus on core competences and may cut costs
questions.explain: Outsourcing frees the firm to concentrate on its core competences and can lower costs through a specialist provider.

questions.q: A firm wanting to increase capacity in the long run could:
options: Invest in new plant and machinery
questions.explain: Investing in additional plant, machinery or premises raises the maximum possible output (capacity).

questions.q: Total Quality Management (TQM) is best characterised as:
options: End-of-line inspection by a quality department
Outsourcing quality checks to a third party
A culture where every employee is responsible for quality
questions.explain: TQM embeds quality as the responsibility of every employee throughout the whole organisation.

questions.q: A key risk of relying on Just-in-Time production is that:
options: Stock becomes obsolete in the warehouse
Too much capital is tied up in stock
A supply-chain disruption can halt production quickly
questions.explain: With minimal buffer stock, any delivery delay or supplier failure can stop production almost immediately.

questions.q: A firm's reorder level is the:
options: Stock level at which a new order is triggered
Maximum stock the warehouse can hold
questions.explain: The reorder level is the inventory point at which a fresh order must be placed to avoid running out.

questions.q: A factory produces 4,000 units using 8 workers in a 40-hour week. What is its labour productivity per worker per hour?
questions.explain: Labour productivity = total output ÷ (workers × hours) = 4,000 ÷ (8 × 40) = 4,000 ÷ 320 = 12.5 units per worker-hour.

questions.q: Holding a buffer (safety) stock of inventory is mainly intended to:
options: Protect against unexpected demand surges or supply delays
questions.explain: Buffer stock provides a cushion against unexpected demand or delivery problems so production and sales can continue.

questions.q: Cell production organises the workforce by:
options: Teams responsible for a complete part or stage of production
One worker completing an entire bespoke job
questions.explain: Cell production groups workers into teams (cells) each responsible for a complete section of the production process.

questions.q: Which is a likely benefit of introducing automation (robotics) into operations?
options: Higher variable labour costs per unit
questions.explain: Automation typically raises productivity and improves consistency of output quality.

questions.q: Quality control differs from quality assurance because quality control:
options: Inspects output to detect defects, often at the end
Builds quality into every stage of the process
Is the responsibility of every worker
questions.explain: Quality control relies on inspecting finished or in-progress output to detect defects, rather than preventing them.

questions.q: A firm achieves productivity gains but quality falls and returns rise. This illustrates:
questions.explain: Pushing output up can compromise quality, showing that operational objectives such as productivity and quality may conflict.

questions.q: A primary purpose of using technology such as CAD/CAM in operations is to:
options: Improve design accuracy and speed up production
questions.explain: CAD/CAM improves design precision and links design to manufacturing, speeding production and cutting errors.

questions.q: Which production method is most associated with high volumes of identical, standardised products on a continuous line?
questions.explain: Flow (mass) production continuously manufactures large volumes of standardised, identical products.

questions.q: Lean production focuses primarily on:
options: Eliminating waste in all forms to add value
Holding excess capacity at all times
questions.explain: Lean production aims to eliminate all forms of waste (time, materials, motion, defects) to maximise value.

questions.q: Which is the most likely consequence of a firm operating persistently at low capacity utilisation?
questions.explain: Spreading fixed costs over fewer units raises the fixed cost per unit, increasing unit costs.

questions.q: A machine can make 600 units per hour but actually makes 480. Its efficiency (utilisation) is:
questions.explain: Efficiency = actual ÷ potential output × 100 = 480 ÷ 600 × 100 = 80%.

questions.q: Which of the following is a diseconomy of scale?
options: Poor communication as the firm grows larger
questions.explain: Communication and coordination problems as a firm grows raise average costs, which is an internal diseconomy of scale.

questions.q: Which of these is an internal economy of scale?
options: A large firm affording specialist managers
Shared research facilities across the industry
A growing pool of skilled labour in the region
Lower industry transport costs available to all firms
questions.explain: Affording specialist managers is a managerial economy internal to the firm; the others are external (industry-wide) economies.

questions.q: A single supplier provides 90% of a manufacturer's components. The main operational risk is:
options: High dependency, so any disruption severely affects production
Too much bargaining power for the manufacturer
questions.explain: Heavy dependence on one supplier means a single disruption can severely interrupt the firm's production.

questions.q: If unit costs fall as output increases over the long run, the firm is experiencing:
questions.explain: A falling long-run average cost as output rises is the definition of economies of scale.

questions.q: The central aim of Just-in-Time (JIT) inventory management is to:
options: Maximise the order quantity to gain discounts
Hold large buffer stocks for safety
Minimise inventory by receiving supplies as needed
questions.explain: JIT minimises inventory-holding by scheduling deliveries to arrive exactly when needed for production.
